Each number was computed correctly. None of them gets from the middle column to the right-hand one without more: for the \(p\)-value, the power of the test and how many of the effects being tested are real; for the fifty states, data on people, or an assumption about them; for the tail, the assumptions of steps 1 and 2 of the variance argument. These are what Feynman called the “details that could throw doubt on your interpretation.”

title: Mindless statistics and sophisticated bigotry
text:
Lenses
You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. “Pretending it was forced is its own failure.” In the null ritual nobody chose the null hypothesis, the level or the test, and nobody has to defend them: its third step is “Always perform this procedure.” In the variance argument the first step is a correct calculation, and the steps after it are stated as if they followed from it.
What are we optimizing or predicting? A state’s rate, or a person’s. A group’s average, or one of its members. The regression on fifty states predicts a state. Statistical discrimination has a person to predict and uses a group’s average.
Who is in the data? Under the two normal curves, about 1 person in 26,000 is four standard deviations out, and the curves were fitted to everyone else. The variance ratios came from fifteen-year-olds in one country or another and ran from 0.95 to 1.24. The ratios in the tail came from one state’s students and from the children who entered a talent search. A feed shows one item in 10,000.
What can be changed, and how? What things are considered “controlled for” or “held fixed,” and is that realistic? Reading the two ends of the fifty-state line as the native-born and foreign-born rates holds each group’s rate fixed from state to state, and the native-born rate was higher in the states where immigrants settled. Calling a variance ratio intrinsic holds it fixed whatever the country, and across countries it ran from 0.95 to 1.24. That challenges a universal ratio; by itself it does not exclude an intrinsic contribution.
And why? Who finds it useful that a group average can be read as a description of a member, or that a feed shows the most extreme item from each group?

Who benefited from that choice being invisible? And would a more competent analyst have chosen differently?

Put both questions to the null ritual and to the variance argument. For the null ritual, Stark and Saltelli’s answer to the first is that cargo-cult statistics “is effective at getting weak work published.” For the variance argument, the calculation was done competently. Would a more competent analyst have taken steps 2 and 3?

title: Mindless statistics and sophisticated bigotry
text:
For the class
The class starts with the two studies of infants. Its optional problems on slopes, ecological regression and bounds use the other three sections. None of the four was in the lecture.

Two studies of infants
You skimmed one of two papers. Connellan, Baron-Cohen, Wheelwright, Batki and Ahluwalia (2000) showed 102 newborns, mean age 37 hours, a face and a mobile, one at a time, and recorded how long each baby looked at each. Alexander, Wilcox and Woods (2009) showed 30 infants aged 3 to 8 months a doll and a toy truck side by side and tracked their eyes. Each paper measured more than one thing and could compare boys and girls on each. The question here is where each comparison was placed: which got the abstract, which got a figure, which got a table, and which got a sentence of text or nothing.
The abstract of Connellan and colleagues says that the boys “showed a stronger interest in the physical-mechanical mobile while the female infants showed a stronger interest in the face,” and ends: “The results of this research clearly demonstrate that sex differences are in part biological in origin.” Table 1 sorts each baby into face preference, mobile preference or no preference. Table 2 gives each sex’s mean percentage of looking time at each stimulus, four means with their standard deviations.









The text reports two tests on Table 2: boys against girls on the mobile, and girls on the face against girls on the mobile. The other two comparisons the same table allows, boys against girls on the face and boys on the face against boys on the mobile, are not reported. The largest group of girls in Table 1 is the 27 of 58 with no preference; the text’s sentence about them is that female babies “either have no preference or prefer the real face.” The evidence offered for the abstract’s last sentence is a chi-squared test on Table 1 (\(p = 0.016\)) and an interaction in Table 2 (\(p = 0.02\)).
In Alexander and colleagues, the eye tracker gave two measures, total looking time and number of fixations. The analysis of variance on looking time did not find a statistically significant sex difference or sex by toy interaction; looking time has three sentences of text and no figure. The analysis of fixations found an interaction, and fixations are what Figure 1 shows and what the abstract reports: the two comparisons that reached significance, of the four the paper set out to test. On the left is the paper’s Figure 1. On the right are the looking times, drawn from the means and standard deviations in the paper’s text in the form the paper used for fixations.






Alexander, Wilcox and Woods (2009), Figure 1: number of fixations.














If you compared the paper’s text with its Figure 1 you may have noticed that they disagree about one comparison: the text says that boys fixated more on the truck than on the doll, a difference that was not significant. An erratum the journal published in 2010 corrects the sentence. Boys fixated more on the doll, as the figure shows.
None of this says that either paper’s result is wrong, and this course makes no claim about whether either has held up. A paper reports some of the comparisons its data allow, and where each one goes, abstract, figure, table, sentence or nowhere, was somebody’s choice. Seeing that some comparisons were given more room than others does not show that the choice was made after looking at the results. In the first paper, 102 babies completed testing; 51 others did not, for crying, falling asleep or fussing.


Two slopes
In the simulation under “Aggregation and \(R^2\)” the slope was the same across areas and across people. The two slopes can differ, and can have opposite signs. For person \(i\) in area \(j\), split both variables into the area average and the deviation from it, \(X_{ij} = \bar X_j + (X_{ij} - \bar X_j)\) and likewise for \(Y\). The deviations average to zero within each area, so the cross terms vanish and \[
\boxed{\;\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \operatorname{Cov}_B + \operatorname{Cov}_W\;}
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{Var}_B + \operatorname{Var}_W ,
\] where \(\operatorname{Cov}_B\) is the covariance between the area averages \(\bar X_j\) and \(\bar Y_j\), with each area weighted by its size, and \(\operatorname{Cov}_W\) is the average of the covariances within areas, weighted the same way. (\(\operatorname{Var}_B\) is the variance of the area averages, which in the model of “Aggregation and \(R^2\)” is \(\sigma_B^2 + \sigma_W^2/n\).) The slope across area averages is \(b_B = \operatorname{Cov}_B / \operatorname{Var}_B\) and the pooled slope within areas is \(b_W = \operatorname{Cov}_W / \operatorname{Var}_W\). The slope across everyone is \[
b_{\text{all}} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}_B + \operatorname{Cov}_W}{\operatorname{Var}_B + \operatorname{Var}_W}
= \lambda\, b_B + (1 - \lambda)\, b_W,
\qquad
\lambda = \frac{\operatorname{Var}_B}{\operatorname{Var}_B + \operatorname{Var}_W} .
\] It is a weighted average of the two slopes, and the weight on the slope between areas is the share of the variance of \(X\) that lies between areas. The three slopes agree when \(b_B = b_W\). When \(b_B\) and \(b_W\) have opposite signs, the sign of \(b_{\text{all}}\) is the sign of \(\operatorname{Cov}_B + \operatorname{Cov}_W\), and knowing the two signs is not enough to say which it is. With \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(b_B = -0.5\) and \(b_W = 0.5\) give \(b_{\text{all}} = 0.40\); the same \(\lambda\) and \(b_W\) with \(b_B = -6\) give \(-0.15\). With a small \(\lambda\), \(b_{\text{all}}\) takes the sign of \(b_B\) only when \(b_B\) is much the steeper of the two.
Gelman, Shor, Bafumi and Park (2007) worked through the US case. In the 2000 and 2004 presidential elections the richer states voted Democratic and the poorer states Republican, which produced years of commentary about affluent liberals and working-class conservatives. Within states, richer voters were more likely to vote Republican, and the same was true across all voters in the country. The authors’ account is the weighted average above: “Income varies far more within states than average income does between states. Consequently, it is the within-state rather than the between-state effect of income that dominates the national patterns.”



Gelman, Shor, Bafumi and Park (2007), Figure 3. Probability of voting for Bush against individual income, in a poor, a middle-income and a rich state. Solid circles: each state’s average income and average support.


The paper’s caption for this figure begins “The paradox is no paradox.” A simulation with the same structure shows the voters as well as the lines.









The dashed line is the regression on everyone. The simulation was built with \(\lambda = 0.14\), a slope between the three state averages of \(-0.6\) and a slope within states of \(0.4\), so the slope for everyone should be about \(0.14(-0.6) + 0.86(0.4) = 0.26\), and the dashed line’s slope is \(0.26\). One slope describes states and the other describes voters.


Ecological regression and the constancy assumption
You want a group’s rate of something, and what you have is area-level data: for each area \(i\), the fraction \(x_i\) of its people who belong to the group, and the fraction \(y_i\) of the same people who have the outcome. (Areas are indexed by \(i\) in this section and the next, as in Freedman’s report.) Fit \[
y_i = a + b x_i + \varepsilon_i
\] by least squares. The height of the line at \(x = 0\) is an area with no group members, so \(\hat a\) is read as the rate among everyone else; the height at \(x = 1\), \(\hat a + \hat b\), as the group’s rate. This is ecological regression (Goodman 1953, 1959). Freedman’s one sentence on its use: it “has been widely used in voting rights litigation in the USA,” where the group is defined by ethnicity, the outcome is a vote, and the ballot is secret.
Write \(p_i\) for the rate among the group’s members in area \(i\) and \(q_i\) for the rate among everyone else. Neither rate is observed. Then \[
y_i = p_i x_i + q_i (1 - x_i)
\] holds by accounting, provided \(x_i\) and \(y_i\) are shares of the same people. (A share of adults and a share of votes cast are shares of different people, and the identity fails for them.) The reading of the line is correct under the constancy assumption: the two rates do not vary systematically with the group’s share of the area. If \(p_i = p\) and \(q_i = q\) in every area, then \(y_i = q + (p - q) x_i\) and the regression recovers \(q\) from its intercept and \(p\) from intercept plus slope. The assumption is about both rates. Area data can sometimes contradict it (a curved scatter, a fitted rate above 1, bounds that rule it out) but cannot confirm it.
When constancy fails, the estimate is wrong in a direction you can compute. In Freedman’s example the regression says 29% and 85% and the truth is 35% and 28%; his explanation is that “the incomes of the native-born increase systematically with fraction of foreign-born in the state,” because immigration concentrates in richer states. Suppose the group’s rate is constant, \(p_i = p\), and everyone else’s rate climbs with the group’s share, \(q_i = q_0 + \gamma x_i\). Substituting, \[
y_i = q_0 + (p - q_0 + \gamma)\, x_i - \gamma x_i^2 .
\] When the shares are small the last term is small, the fitted slope is close to \(p - q_0 + \gamma\), and the line at \(x = 1\) is close to \(p + \gamma\): the gradient in everyone else’s rate has been added to the group’s rate. How much of \(\gamma\) is added depends on how the shares are distributed: in the two-area example below it is about seven tenths.









The figure is a simulation with that structure, fifty areas of equal size and a little noise in everyone else’s rate, with numbers chosen so that the fitted line resembles Freedman’s: \(p = 0.28\), \(q_0 = 0.29\), \(\gamma = 0.7\). The regression reports the group’s rate as 0.84 when it is 0.28 in every area, and everyone else’s rate as 0.30 when over all areas it is 0.36. Freedman says that the trouble is not that the line has been extended beyond the data: “the same sort of reversal can occur even with a full spectrum of \(x\)-values. The issue is the disaggregation, not the range of the data.”
A version small enough to do by hand: two areas of equal size at \(x = 0.1\) and \(x = 0.2\), with \(p = 0.28\), \(q_0 = 0.30\) and \(\gamma = 0.5\). The area rates are \(0.343\) and \(0.376\), the line through them is \(y = 0.31 + 0.33x\), and the group’s rate it reports is \(0.64\) against a truth of \(0.28\). It reports everyone else’s rate as \(0.31\); over the two areas it is \(0.374\). This error is a bias. It does not shrink as areas get larger or more numerous: more data with the same assumption gives the same wrong answer with a smaller standard error. The constancy assumption is the kind Stark and Saltelli mean when they write of “the mechanical application of methods without understanding their assumptions, limitations, or interpretation.” It is stated nowhere in the regression output, and in the figure above nothing in the output shows that it has failed.
Freedman’s Table 2, in section 5 of the report, which you were not asked to read, sets four answers side by side.









The neighborhood model assumes the opposite of constancy: everyone in an area has the area’s rate, \(\hat p_i = \hat q_i = y_i\), whatever group they belong to. For the income data it estimates 34% and 36% against the truth of 35% and 28%, far closer than ecological regression’s 29% and 85%. The fourth method is the random-coefficients model of King (1997), in which the two rates vary from area to area but are drawn from one distribution whatever the area’s makeup: a version of the constancy assumption, as Freedman says. Freedman does not conclude that the neighborhood model is right. “In some contexts, of course, the neighborhood model proves deficient. If the data are incomplete so estimation is needed, it will be unclear which model if any is giving the right answers.” Every one of these models is compatible with the fifty points, so the points cannot show which assumption holds.


The method of bounds
Freedman’s section 4, optional in the reading list.
There is one thing the area data do settle without any assumption. Freedman’s example: in Washington state in 1995, 7.9% of adults were foreign-born and 34.4% had high incomes. Write \(p\) for the high-income rate among the foreign-born and \(q\) for the rate among the native-born. The accounting identity \[
0.079\,p + 0.921\,q = 0.344
\] is one equation in two unknowns. But \(p\) is between 0 and 1, so \(q\) is trapped: \[
q = \frac{0.344 - 0.079\,p}{0.921} \in
\left[\frac{0.344 - 0.079}{0.921},\ \frac{0.344}{0.921}\right] = [0.288,\ 0.374].
\]









Every point on the line segment reproduces the two percentages we were given. Its slope is \(-0.079/0.921\), nearly flat, because the foreign-born are a small share of the state: \(q\) is pinned to a narrow band and \(p\) can be anything from 0 to 1. In general, for area \(i\), \[
q_i \in \left[\max\!\left(0, \frac{y_i - x_i}{1 - x_i}\right),\
\min\!\left(1, \frac{y_i}{1 - x_i}\right)\right],
\qquad
p_i \in \left[\max\!\left(0, \frac{y_i - (1 - x_i)}{x_i}\right),\
\min\!\left(1, \frac{y_i}{x_i}\right)\right].
\] These are the Duncan–Davis bounds (1953). The interval for \(p_i\) has width \(\min(x_i,\, 1 - x_i,\, y_i,\, 1 - y_i)/x_i\), and the interval for \(q_i\) has the same numerator over \(1 - x_i\). So the bounds on a group’s rate are the whole of \([0, 1]\) when the group is smaller than both the share of people with the outcome and the share without it, as the foreign-born are in Washington. They are not always wide for a small group. If a group is 5% of an area and 2% of the area’s people have the outcome, the group’s rate is at most \(0.02/0.05 = 0.4\).
Any estimate narrower than the bounds gets its extra precision from an assumption. Freedman notes that “in many applications, the bounds are too broad to be informative,” which is why people reach for a model.

title: Mindless statistics and sophisticated bigotry
text:
Readings
As announced. There are several, but they are short, and part of the work is deciding when to scan and when to slow down.

Required

Stark and Saltelli, Cargo-cult statistics and scientific crisis (Significance 15, 2018, 40–43). Four pages, open access; read it in full.
Hyde and Mertz, Gender, culture, and mathematics performance (PNAS 106, 2009, 8801–8807; free full text at Europe PMC). Read the first paragraph of the section “Do Gender Differences Exist Among the Mathematically Talented?” and understand Figure 1 and Table 2.
Freedman, Ecological Inference and the Ecological Fallacy (Berkeley Statistics Technical Report 549, 1999). Sections 1 to 3; section 4, the method of bounds, is optional. Read the PDF at this link; a much shorter 2002 entry by Freedman with a similar title circulates online and has none of the worked example.
One of two psychology studies, as announced: Connellan, Baron-Cohen, Wheelwright, Batki and Ahluwalia, “Sex differences in human neonatal social perception” (Infant Behavior and Development 23, 2000, 113–118), or Alexander, Wilcox and Woods, Sex Differences in Infants’ Visual Interest in Toys (Archives of Sexual Behavior 38, 2009, 427–433). Skim it with attention to the data and the statistical analysis, and form your own guess about whether its results would be reproduced.



Optional

Rathje, Van Bavel and van der Linden, Out-group animosity drives engagement on social media (PNAS 118, 2021).
Gigerenzer and Marewski, Surrogate Science: The Idol of a Universal Method for Scientific Inference (Journal of Management 41, 2015, 421–440; LSE library access). The phrase “mindless statistics” is Gigerenzer’s, from a 2004 paper of that title.

Cited in the text and not assigned: Feynman, “Cargo Cult Science” (1974); Schwartz, “The Pernicious Influence of Mathematics on Science” (1962); Gigerenzer, “Mindless statistics” (Journal of Socio-Economics 33, 2004, 587–606), which reports Oakes (1986) and Haller and Krauss (2002); Franco, Blau and Zimbardo (2011), as quoted by Gigerenzer and Marewski; Robinson (1950); Bradford Hill, “The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?” (Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine 58, 1965, 295–300); Phelps, “The Statistical Theory of Racism and Sexism” (American Economic Review 62, 1972, 659–661); Arrow, “The Theory of Discrimination” (in Discrimination in Labor Markets, 1973); Goodman (1953, 1959); Duncan and Davis (1953); King, A Solution to the Ecological Inference Problem (1997); Gelman, Shor, Bafumi and Park (2007); Hyde, Lindberg, Linn, Ellis and Williams (2008), whose data Hyde and Mertz’s Table 1 summarizes; Machin and Pekkarinen (2008), whose variance ratios their Table 2 reports; the erratum to Alexander and colleagues, Archives of Sexual Behavior 39 (2010), 816.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Exercises
The exercises can be done by hand, except the last three, which use R. Attempt each part before you open a hint.






WarningHints



Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order.



Exercise 1. Omitted-variable bias
In the linear model of the notes, \(Z := U_Z\), \(X := \alpha Z + U_X\), \(Y := \beta X + \gamma Z + U_Y\), with independent mean-zero noise, take \(\alpha = 2\), \(\gamma = 1\), \(\beta = 0.5\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \operatorname{Var}(U_X) = 1\).

Compute \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z)\) and the slope of \(Y\) on \(X\) alone.
Repeat with \(\gamma = -1\).
Repeat with \(\gamma = 1\) and \(\beta = 0\). What would someone with data on \(X\) and \(Y\) alone conclude?
Is the error in (a) a bias or a variance? What happens to it as the sample grows?







TipHint 1





\(Z\) and \(U_X\) are independent, so \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(Z) + \operatorname{Var}(U_X)\).





Exercise 2. Choosing an adjustment set










List the backdoor paths from \(X\) to \(Y\).
Which of these sets satisfy the backdoor criterion: the empty set, \(\{Z\}\), \(\{M\}\), \(\{Z, M\}\), \(\{W\}\), \(\{Z, W\}\)?
In a linear model, what does the coefficient on \(X\) estimate if you adjust for \(\{Z, M\}\)?
If more than one of the sets in (b) satisfies the criterion, which would you use, and why?







TipHint 1





A backdoor path starts with an arrow into \(X\). How many arrows point into \(X\)?





Exercise 3. The graph behind an argument
A university says: “Students who use the library more get better grades. We will extend the library’s opening hours, because using the library improves grades.”

Draw the causal graph the argument presupposes, and mark the action.
Add one variable that would make the observed difference larger than the effect, with its arrows.
What comparison would support the university’s claim?







TipHint 1





The university’s evidence compares students. Its action changes opening hours. Are those the same thing?





Exercise 4. Hormone therapy
The notes’ section on hormone therapy and heart disease gives three studies of whether to prescribe hormone therapy to prevent heart disease. Two of them are Grodstein and colleagues (1996) and Hernán and colleagues (2008).

Write the decision with \(X\) and \(Y\). Say what the treatment and the outcome are, and write the quantity a doctor needs with \(do(\cdot)\).
The 1996 estimate (0.39) and the 2008 intention-to-treat estimates (1.42 over the first two years, 0.96 over the whole follow-up) come from the same cohort, the Nurses’ Health Study. Which comparison did each make?
Draw a graph under which the 1996 estimate is confounded.
Which comparison matches the decision a doctor makes, and why?







TipHint 1





For (a), what does the doctor choose, and which outcome is the choice about? For (b), ask which two groups each analysis compares.





Exercise 5. Prediction and intervention, in R
Open a fresh R script. You will need the tidyverse.

n <- 10000
# program 1: X causes Y
X1 <- rnorm(n); Y1 <- 2 * X1 + rnorm(n)
# program 2: Z causes both
Z2 <- rnorm(n); X2 <- Z2 + rnorm(n); Y2 <- Z2 + rnorm(n)
# program 3: X causes Y through M
X3 <- sqrt(2) * rnorm(n); M3 <- X3 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n); Y3 <- 0.5 * M3 + rnorm(n)


Write down the slope of \(Y\) on \(X\) you expect in each program. Then fit lm and compare.
For each program, intervene: set \(X\) to 1 for everyone and run the statements after the one for \(X\) again, then the same with \(X\) set to 0. Compute the difference in the means of \(Y\).
In program 2, fit lm(Y2 ~ X2 + Z2). In program 3, fit lm(Y3 ~ X3 + M3). Compare the coefficients on \(X\) with your answers to 2.







TipHint 1





In each program, which statements after the one for \(X\) use \(X\), directly or through a variable computed from it? Those are the ones whose values change when you set \(X\).





Exercise 6. Adjustment on data, in R
The table of problem 1, one row for each rider.

cells <- data.frame(Z = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                    W = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0),
                    T = c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0),
                    n = c(70, 30, 100, 100, 80, 120, 50, 450),
                    accidents = c(21, 12, 10, 15, 4, 18, 1, 18))
# In base R, T means TRUE; inside dplyr verbs, T is the column
riders <- bind_rows(
  cells |> mutate(Y = 1, count = accidents),
  cells |> mutate(Y = 0, count = n - accidents)
) |>
  select(Z, W, T, Y, count) |>
  tidyr::uncount(count)
nrow(riders)

[1] 1000



Compute the share with an accident among riders who took the course and among those who did not, from riders, and the difference.
Compute the adjusted difference: the difference within each combination of \(Z\) and \(W\), averaged with weights \(P(Z = z, W = w)\). Then adjust for \(Z\) alone, and for \(W\) alone.
A randomized version: give each of the 1,000 riders the course with probability 0.3, whatever their group, and draw whether they have an accident from the table’s rates. Compute the difference. Repeat 200 times. What is the average difference, and how much does it vary?







TipHint 1





For 2: riders |> group_by(Z, W) |> summarize(...) gives one row for each group of riders; compute the difference and the group’s share of all riders there.





Exercise 7. Intervening in a program, in R
The job center from the lecture, as a program. As in the lecture, everyone referred attends and nobody else does. Each line generates one variable from the ones above it.

n <- 10000
Z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                        # worked last year
X <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.8, 0.2))   # attended the course
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X + 0.3 * Z)    # in work six months later
mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0])             # attenders against the others


Run it. Compare the difference with the lecture’s first job-center table (64% against 36%).
Compute the adjusted difference: the difference between attenders and non-attenders within \(Z = 1\) and within \(Z = 0\), averaged with weights mean(Z == 1) and mean(Z == 0).
Intervene. Replace the line for X by X <- rep(1, n), run the line for Y again, and record mean(Y). Do the same with X <- rep(0, n). Compare the difference with your answer to 2.
The center changes its referrals to 0.95 for \(Z = 1\) and 0.05 for \(Z = 0\). Before you run anything, write down what you expect for the differences in 1 and in 3. Then run it.







TipHint 1





For step 3, replace the line for X and leave the line for Z alone. Then run the line for Y again, so that it uses the new X.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
In class

Discussion 1: absurd trolley problems
In your group, open Absurd Trolley Problems on one device and play for about six minutes, choosing together. Note the scenarios where the group disagreed, and the ones you personally found hard to choose.

Take one scenario where the group disagreed. Which framework was each side using?
Did any of your choices depend on a prediction of what would happen? How sure of it were you?



Discussion 2: a model that decides about people
Think of a scenario in which a predictive algorithm is deployed to make, or help to make, decisions with large effects on people: which applicants get a loan, which patients a GP sees first, which benefit claims are checked for fraud. Choose one in your group.

Describe the scenario: who uses the model, what it predicts, from what data, and what is decided with it.
Decide what features or mechanisms would have to be in place to satisfy the four Belmont–Menlo principles (National Commission 1979; Dittrich and Kenneally 2012) and the five Cs of Patil, Mason and Loukides (2018): consent; clarity; consistency and trust; control and transparency; consequences. Say which principle or C each one serves.
Which of your requirements is about an effect, so that checking it needs a causal claim?

At the end, each group describes its scenario and its requirements to the other groups.


The adjustment formula, from memory
Before the problems, from memory: what does the adjustment formula average, and with what weights?


Problem 1. A safety course for riders
A food-delivery platform offers its riders a road-safety course. It pushes the course hardest to new riders and to riders who work mostly at night. New riders have more accidents than experienced riders, by day and by night, and night work raises accidents for both. New riders, who book their shifts last, more often work at night. Assume that nothing else affects both taking the course and having an accident. The platform’s records for 1,000 riders, with \(Z = 1\) for a rider who had joined in the three months before the course was offered, \(W = 1\) for one who then worked mostly at night, \(T = 1\) for one who took the course and \(Y = 1\) for one who had an accident in the six months after:

Draw the graph with \(T\), \(Y\), \(Z\) and \(W\). Which set of variables satisfies the backdoor criterion for the effect of \(T\) on \(Y\)?
Compute the share who had an accident among riders who took the course and among those who did not.
Compute \(P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 1))\) and \(P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 0))\) with the adjustment formula, and the average treatment effect.
A manager proposes to drop the course, citing (b). An analyst who adjusts only for whether riders are new finds that the course lowers the chance of an accident by about 2.5 percentage points. What would you tell each of them?



Problem 2. Backdoor paths
In each graph, \(T\) is the treatment and \(Y\) the outcome.









A path is blocked by a set of variables if somewhere along it

a fork, \(\leftarrow V \to\), or a chain, \(\to V \to\) or \(\leftarrow V \leftarrow\), has its middle variable \(V\) in the set, or
a collider, \(\to V \leftarrow\), has neither \(V\) nor any descendant of \(V\) in the set.

The second rule is the reading’s (Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan 2023, pp. 115–116): a path through a collider is blocked when you adjust for nothing, and adjusting for the collider opens it.

For each graph, list the backdoor paths from \(T\) to \(Y\). Which of them are open when you adjust for nothing?
For each graph, find a smallest set of variables that satisfies the backdoor criterion for the effect of \(T\) on \(Y\). Is it the only one of that size?
In graph 2, an analyst adjusts for \(C\), because \(C\) was measured before \(T\) and “adjusting for more can’t hurt.” Which path does that open? Suppose \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are yes-or-no variables, \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, and \(A = 1\) or \(B = 1\) is enough to make \(C = 1\), as either disease was enough for admission to hospital in the reading’s example (p. 113). Among people with \(C = 1\), are \(A\) and \(B\) associated, and in which direction?
In graph 3, only \(C\) was measured. Can the effect of \(T\) on \(Y\) be estimated by adjusting for measured variables?



Discussion 3: the case for one framework
The room splits into three groups. Each group develops an argument for one statement and presents it to the other groups.

Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly on consequentialist ethics.
Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly on deontological ethics.
Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly on virtue ethics.

You have 15 minutes to develop your argument and 2 minutes to present it. Think about how to structure it to convince the listener, and answer the strongest objection to it. The group arguing for consequentialism should also answer this question: does it become more or less defensible once you have to write the causal model down?
Then everyone votes for the account they find most convincing, which need not be the one their group argued for: consequentialist, deontological or virtue ethics for data science and AI, a combination, or none of them?

title: Ethics and causation
text:
If there is time

One sentence, individually: what is the difference between \(P(Y = 1 \mid T = 1)\) and \(P(Y = 1 \mid do(T := 1))\)?
The reading (p. 113) warns against judging an admissions test by how well it predicts success among the students who were admitted. Draw the graph. Where is the collider?
“Correlation (more generally, association) is not causation.” This is true and important, but can it be misused?
Can causality be useful in the context of reproducibility? In designing and communicating studies?
A company tests two versions of its app on its users, without telling them, to see which version keeps them using the app longer. Which of the Belmont–Menlo principles does this touch? How would each framework judge it?
Find a sentence in a news report of an observational study that avoids saying “causes” but implies a cause. What graph does it assume?

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Normative ethics: four frameworks









judges an action by
a difficulty




Consequentialism
its effects
predicting consequences


Deontology
whether it follows a rule or a duty
a rule kept where it leads somewhere terrible


Virtue ethics
the character it expresses
virtues conflict


Pragmatic ethics
norms held like hypotheses, revised by inquiry
how people judge, or how they should?



These approaches are not mutually exclusive or exhaustive, so we do not have to choose one of them or limit our thinking to using only these ideas.

ms4ds, section 3.2.2 (the last line) and sections 3.2.2.1 to 3.2.2.3 (the first three rows); Wikipedia, Deontology and Pragmatic ethics.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Which framework?
A hospital is deciding whether to use a model to choose which patients get a follow-up call after discharge.

“A good doctor would not hand that judgment to a score.”
“Use it. In the pilot, readmissions fell.”
“Try it on one ward, watch what happens, and change the rules as we learn.”
“Don’t. Patients never agreed to their records being used this way.”


Which framework is each argument using? Which of them would you need data to settle?

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Consequentialism

An act is right “if and only if the act […] will produce, will probably produce, or is intended to produce, a greater balance of good over evil than any available alternative.”


Wikipedia, Consequentialism.










Causal understanding is necessary to apply consequentialism.

ms4ds, section 3.4.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Utilitarianism
Bentham and Mill: choose the action that does the most good, adding up everyone’s happiness.







a difficulty
in data science




defining utility
choosing the outcome, the metric or the loss


trading off between people
adding gains and losses across people


judging acts or rules
one decision, or the model that makes them all


predicting consequences
effects of actions, not associations




ms4ds, section 3.2.2.1 (the four difficulties); Wikipedia, Consequentialism.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Utilitarian language
Data science is usually framed (perhaps implicitly) as utilitarian because of its focus on prediction/causation (consequences) and optimization (utility).

ms4ds, section 3.2.2, discussion questions.


Choose a data science task: a recommender, a credit score, an A/B test. Say it in utilitarian language: whose good, measured how, added up over who? Then give one objection a deontologist or a virtue ethicist would make.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
The Belmont and Menlo principles









In the Tuskegee study, Black men with syphilis were never told they had it and were kept from treatment after penicillin was known to work.

Beneficence, in the Menlo Report’s words: “Do not harm; Maximize probable benefits and minimize probable harms; Systematically assess both risk of harm and benefit.”


ms4ds, section 3.3.1, which quotes the Menlo Report (2012); Wikipedia, Belmont Report.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
The five Cs








asks




Consent
did people explicitly agree, knowing what will be collected and what for?


Clarity
do they understand what their consent allows?


Consistency and trust
does the system behave as people expect?


Control and transparency
can they see the status of their data, and opt in or out of particular uses later?


Consequences
what unintended harm could the data do, to children for example, or by linking sources to identify people?




Loukides, Mason and Patil, Ethics and Data Science, as summarized in ms4ds, section 3.3.2.

section: Observational studies that recommend a practice

Observational studies that recommend a practice

text:
Structural causal models

“a sequence of assignments for generating a joint distribution starting from independent noise variables.”










\(Z\) a common cause, \(M\) a mediator, \(C\) a common effect.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Exercise, weight and heart disease
\(U_1 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/2)\), \(\;U_2, U_3 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/3)\), independent; \(\mathrm{Ber}(q)\) is 1 with probability \(q\).



\(X := U_1\) (exercise)
\(W :=\) if \(X = 1\) then \(0\) else \(U_2\) (overweight)
\(H :=\) if \(X = 1\) then \(0\) else \(U_3\) (heart disease)












Apart from the noise, an arrow into a variable comes from each variable its line uses: \(W\) and \(H\) are both computed from \(X\).

Compute \(P(H = 1)\) and \(P(H = 1 \mid W = 1)\).


fairmlbook, chapter 5, “A first example.”

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Conditioning and intervening
\(P(H = 1) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac16\), \(\qquad P(H = 1 \mid W = 1) = \tfrac13\).


\(do(W := 1)\): replace line 2 by \(W := 1\). In the graph, the arrow into \(W\) is deleted.
\(P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 1)) = \tfrac16\).












“The substitution \(W := 1\) does not correspond to a conditioning on \(W = 1\). One is an action, albeit inconsequential in this case.”

\(X\) and \(Y\) are confounded when \(P(Y = y \mid do(X := x)) \ne P(Y = y \mid X = x)\).

fairmlbook, chapter 5, “A first example” and “Confounding.”

title: Ethics and causation
text:
The average treatment effect
\[
\text{ATE} = E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] - E[Y \mid do(X := 0)]
\]
\(X\) set to 1 for everyone, against \(X\) set to 0 for everyone, with the arrows into \(X\) deleted.
\[
E[Y \mid X = 1] - E[Y \mid X = 0]
\]
The observed difference: the people who happened to be treated, against those who were not.

“Causal effects are population quantities.”


fairmlbook, chapter 5, “Causal effects.”

Adding up over people
If gains add up across people, and nobody’s outcome depends on anyone else’s treatment, treating all \(n\) rather than none changes the expected total by \(n \times \text{ATE}\): the utilitarian’s comparison.










Belmont’s justice: who gets the benefits of research, and who bears its burdens? For a policy, what would you need besides the ATE?

Prediction and intervention










“If we expect a model to also tell us what happens when we intervene on variables, then […] models with equal predictive accuracy are no longer equivalent. We become responsible to choose one of them.”

title: Ethics and causation
text:
The adjustment formula
\(Z\) worked last year, \(X\) attended, \(Y\) in work. \(do(X := 1)\) deletes the arrow \(Z \to X\), and \(Z\) keeps its distribution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] &= \sum_z E[Y \mid X = 1, Z = z]\,P(Z = z) \\
&= 0.7 \times 0.5 + 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.55 \\
E[Y \mid do(X := 0)] &= 0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.45
\end{aligned}
\]
The average treatment effect is \(0.10\).

\(P(Y = y \mid do(X := x)) = \sum_z P(Y = y \mid X = x, Z = z)\,P(Z = z)\) when \(Z\) satisfies the backdoor criterion (later in the lecture), and every value of \(Z\) includes people with \(X = x\).

title: Ethics and causation
text:
The observed comparison
\(Z\) worked last year, \(X\) attended, \(Y\) in work. Each row is weighted by its share of attenders, or of non-attenders:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) &= \frac{0.7 \times 400 + 0.4 \times 100}{500} = 0.64 \\
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) &= \frac{0.6 \times 100 + 0.3 \times 400}{500} = 0.36
\end{aligned}
\]
Attenders come mostly from the \(Z = 1\) row, where more people find work whether or not they attend.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Referral at random
Same people, same rows. The center now refers half of each row, chosen at random; everyone referred attends, and nobody else does.

Compute the share in work you would expect among those who attended, and among those who did not. Compare the difference with the average treatment effect.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Randomization
Half of each row attends, chosen at random. The shares to expect:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) &= 0.5 \times 0.7 + 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.55 \\
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) &= 0.5 \times 0.6 + 0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.45
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference to expect is \(0.55 - 0.45 = 0.10\), the average treatment effect. Any one randomization gives a difference near \(0.10\), and a different random draw would give a slightly different number.

“The goal of a randomized controlled trial is to break natural inclination.”


fairmlbook, chapter 5, “Randomization.”

title: Ethics and causation
text:
The backdoor criterion
A backdoor path from \(X\) to \(Y\) starts with an arrow into \(X\): here, \(X \leftarrow Z \to Y\).
\(Z\) satisfies the backdoor criterion if

no variable in \(Z\) is a descendant of \(X\), and
\(Z\) blocks every backdoor path from \(X\) to \(Y\).

A path through a fork or a chain is blocked by conditioning on the variable in the middle.

Controlling for a mediator “will eliminate some of the causal influence of \(X\) on \(Y\).”


The criterion: Pearl (2009), Causality, as cited in fairmlbook, chapter 5. The quotation: fairmlbook, chapter 5, “Confounding.”

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Unobserved confounding












\(U\): something unmeasured, such as motivation, that pushes people onto the course and into work.
Under the graph without \(U\), adjusting for \(Z\) gives the effect. Under this one, the back door through \(U\) stays open, and the 10 points probably overstates the effect.
The data on \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) fit both graphs.

title: Ethics and causation
text:
Lenses this week

Which comparison gets reported? Attenders against non-attenders, overall or within rows. The average effect, or the effects within groups defined before treatment.
You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. The adjustment set follows from a graph you drew. The backdoor criterion says which sets are valid given the graph. “Pretending it was forced is its own failure.”
What can be changed, and how? Adjusting for worked last year holds it fixed while attendance is set. Adjusting for a mediator holds fixed something the course would change. Randomization makes “held fixed” true by design.

…and why?

title: What’s the score?
text: Important note: this week’s examples include a commercial product and two platforms. Where I say what a company did, the source is the paper or the company’s own statement, linked. Where I say what it should have done, the view is mine, and a well-argued position I think is wrong can still get full marks.

title: What’s the score?
text:
Summary
A score is a number computed about a person and used to decide something about them. The number measures one thing, \(Y\), and is taken to stand for another, \(Y^\star\). The two come apart in three ways: noise, an offset that differs between groups, and a response by the people being measured. A health system’s risk score measured next year’s medical cost and was taken to stand for how ill a patient was; at the same cost, Black patients were sicker, so the score flagged fewer of them for extra care, and the ones it did flag were sicker than the White patients it flagged. In a model with an offset \(\beta_A\) for one group, selecting above a threshold \(t\) on the measure is selecting above \(t - \beta_A\) on the thing measured, for that group only.
Once a score is rewarded, the people and systems it is applied to act on the score. That changes the equation for \(Y\), an intervention, and what \(Y\) says about \(Y^\star\) afterward is not what it said before. Strategic classification and performative prediction are two formal versions of this. Reinforcement learning says the same thing in other letters: an agent is given a reward \(R\), and the good we care about is a utility \(U\).

title: What’s the score?
text:
Scores

Citation counts
The significance filter is one selection: of the tests that were run, the ones with \(p < 0.05\) were the ones that reached print. The same filter operates further down the pipeline. De Vries and colleagues (2018) took 105 trials of antidepressants that drug companies had registered with the US Food and Drug Administration, which classified 53 as positive and 52 as negative or questionable, and followed them into the literature.





Of the 105 trials, 77 were published: 98% of the positive trials and 48% of the negative ones. Ten negative trials appeared positive in print after an unfavorable outcome was dropped or a secondary outcome promoted to primary. Of the 77 published, 4 said plainly that the drug had not beaten placebo. And in the literature as cited, positive trials were cited about three times as often as negative ones, 92 citations to 32 on average. Each panel is a selection, and each selection runs the same way. The file-drawer effect turns variance into bias.
A citation count is a score. It is what a researcher’s output is measured by, and it is taken to stand for a contribution to knowledge. The figure shows the two coming apart stage by stage: at each stage, more of the positive results survive. The paper documents the selections; it says nothing about anyone’s intentions.


What a score does to the people it is applied to
The citation count also does something to the people it measures. A researcher who knows that positive results are published and cited has a reason to find one, and p-hacking is a way of finding one. What a score does to the people who write for it is a different mechanism from selection.
The usual name for this is Goodhart’s law. Charles Goodhart, in a 1975 paper on monetary management in the United Kingdom, wrote that “Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.” The quotation is the one the Wikipedia article gives, from the paper’s 1981 reprint, page 116; the paper itself was not available to check. The wording most people know is Marilyn Strathern’s, from a 1997 paper on auditing British universities: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure” (Strathern 1997, p. 308).
Manheim and Garrabrant (2018) sort the ways this happens into four. Their regressional case is the one the next section derives: a proxy that is the goal plus noise overstates the goal wherever the proxy is large. Their adversarial case is the one the section on systems that adapt takes up: once the measure is rewarded, other people, with aims of their own, act on it. In their causal case the regulator’s own intervention on the proxy changes its relation to the goal, and in their extremal case an optimizer pushes the system into a region where the old relation does not hold; both are named here and not developed.


Measured and intended
Write \(Y\) for the outcome a system measures and \(Y^\star\) for the one it was meant to measure: the one we would use if we could. In a regression \(Y\) is the response; in a classifier it is the label; in a reward signal it is the number the agent is given.







\(Y\), measured
\(Y^\star\), intended




citations
contribution to knowledge


\(p < 0.05\)
a true effect


a job center’s placement rate
people in work because of it


a patient’s medical cost
how ill the patient is


a video’s views
a viewer informed, or entertained, on their own terms



The two differ by three routes.

Noise. \(Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\) unrelated to anything else. A noisy measure is still right on average, but a slope on it is flattened toward zero.
An offset that differs between groups. \(Y = Y^\star + \beta_A A\), with \(A\) a group and \(\beta_A \ne 0\). The measure is right on average for one group and off by \(\beta_A\) for the other, and selecting on it selects the groups differently.
A response to being measured. Once \(Y\) is rewarded, the people and systems it is applied to act on \(Y\) itself. The equation for \(Y\) changes.

The first lens asks about every row of the table: what are we optimizing or predicting? The answer “cost” or “views” is correct and incomplete. The next question is what the number was taken to stand for, and who decided that it could.

title: What’s the score?
section: Cost as a proxy for need
text:
Cost as a proxy for need

A risk score in health care
Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli and Mullainathan (2019) studied a commercial risk score at a large academic hospital. The score was used to decide which patients were offered extra care. Patients above the 97th percentile of the score were identified for a care-management program automatically; patients above the 55th were flagged to their doctor. Whether an identified patient was then enrolled was a decision for clinicians, so the paper’s numbers are about identification, and these notes say “selected” for it. The score was a prediction of each patient’s medical costs in the coming year, and race was not one of its inputs. By industry estimates, the authors write, tools of this class are applied to roughly 200 million people in the United States each year.
The sample was patients in primary care at the hospital from 2013 to 2015: 6,079 Black patients and 43,539 White patients, counted over 11,929 and 88,080 patient-years. A patient-year is one patient’s data for one calendar year. The authors could see each patient’s score and their health records.
At a given score, Black and White patients cost about the same in the following year, which is what a cost model should deliver. At a given score, Black patients were sicker. The paper’s Figure 1A plots the number of active chronic conditions against the score’s percentile, one curve per group, and the paper reports that at the same score Black patients had more illness. At the 97th percentile, the automatic-enrollment point, Black patients averaged 4.8 active chronic conditions and White patients 3.8, 26% more.









Why? At the same number of chronic conditions, Black patients in the sample generated about $1,801 less in medical costs a year, and everyone in the sample was insured. The authors name two routes. Barriers to care: poverty, geography, transport, the demands of work and child care, and knowing when to seek care, all of which reduce spending at a given level of illness. And the effect of race on the care a patient receives once they are seen; the paper cites a trial (its reference 32) that found higher uptake of recommended preventive care when the doctor was Black. Either way, cost measures need with an offset that depends on race.
The authors simulate what removing the gap would do. The share of Black patients among those identified automatically would rise from 17.7% to 46.5%. Separately, they trained new models on three labels. With total cost as the label, Black patients were 14.1% of the highest-risk group (the 97th percentile and above); with avoidable cost, 21.0%; with the number of active chronic conditions, 26.7%. The label is the choice, and the paper is about what that one choice did.
The paper’s abstract describes the first figure as “the percentage of Black patients receiving additional help,” which is not what was computed; the body gives the Black share of patients auto-identified at the 97th percentile. A paper about a loosely specified target whose abstract loosely specifies its own number is the first lens applied to the paper that teaches it. Read the body.


A model: an offset for one group
Take need \(Y^\star\) to have the same distribution in both groups (an assumption, not a finding: see below), and let \(A = 1\) for one group and \(0\) for the other. The measure is \[
Y = Y^\star + \beta_A A ,
\] and the program selects everyone with \(Y > t\). For group \(0\) that is \(Y^\star > t\). For group \(1\) it is \(Y^\star + \beta_A > t\), or \(Y^\star > t - \beta_A\). An offset of \(\beta_A\) in the measure is a threshold moved by \(-\beta_A\) for that group. With \(\beta_A < 0\), as in the paper, group \(1\) has to be iller to be selected.









Two things follow, and both are in the paper’s data.
Who is selected. Group \(1\) is selected with probability \(P(Y^\star > t - \beta_A)\) and group \(0\) with probability \(P(Y^\star > t)\). With \(Y^\star \sim N(0, 1)\) and \(t\) the 97th percentile, \(t = 1.88\):

An offset of half a standard deviation cuts group \(1\)’s chance of selection to less than a third of group \(0\)’s. In percentage points the gap is small, 3.0 against 0.9; at the median the same offset would move the shares from 50% to 31%, a gap of 19 points but a ratio of only 0.62. A threshold in the tail turns a small offset into a large proportional disparity, because the normal density falls quickly there.
How ill the selected are. The mean of a standard normal variable given that it exceeds \(z\) is \[
E[Y^\star \mid Y^\star > z] = \frac{\phi(z)}{1 - \Phi(z)} ,
\] the inverse Mills ratio, which also gave the expected size of an estimate that survived the significance filter. Here it gives the mean need of the selected in each group: \(z = t\) for group \(0\) and \(z = t - \beta_A\) for group \(1\). Since the ratio increases in \(z\), the selected members of group \(1\) are iller on average than the selected members of group \(0\), by about half a standard deviation in the second row of the table.
The paper’s Figure 1A compares a different quantity: need at a given score, not above a threshold. In this model that comparison is simpler. Two patients with the same measure \(Y = y\) have needs \(y\) and \(y - \beta_A\), so at every score group \(1\) is iller by \(-\beta_A\), and the gap does not depend on where the threshold is. The table’s comparison, among the selected, adds the tail effect on top: group \(1\)’s selected members are drawn from further out in the need distribution.
This is a bias, and more data does not touch it. A larger sample estimates the offset more precisely and selects the same people.
The model assumes need has the same distribution in both groups. In the paper’s sample it does not (Black patients were on average sicker), which is why the paper’s shares are what they are rather than the table’s; the direction of both effects is the same. The model also assumes the offset is the same for everyone in group \(1\), when in the paper it comes from barriers that vary from person to person. Read the table as a mechanism, not as the hospital’s numbers.


Who bears the error
A threshold makes two kinds of mistake. A patient can be selected without needing the program, which uses a place and the program’s time. A patient can be left out while needing it, which costs the patient. Setting \(t\) at the 97th percentile rather than the 90th trades the two: fewer places used, more people left out. The threshold fixes the trade without saying how it was valued; a budget for places would fix it too.

The offset moves the second error onto one group. For a Black patient at the enrollment threshold, the score says “not ill enough” at a level of illness at which it says “selected” for a White patient. The price of an error is paid by the person it falls on, and the offset determines who that is. The fourth lens asks who bears the error; here the answer is the group whose costs were lower at the same need.
Then the standing question. Who benefited from that choice being invisible? The tool predicted cost, and the authors call that choice reasonable, since “the program’s goal, at least in part, is to reduce costs” (Obermeyer and colleagues 2019, “Problem formulation”). Nobody had to decide that cost stood for need; the label did it for them. And would a more competent analyst have chosen differently? The paper’s own answer is yes, in a specific way: the program mostly prevents acute episodes in people with chronic illness, so avoidable cost or the number of chronic conditions would have measured what the program was for, and the authors worked with the manufacturer to change the label.


A noisy measure flattens a slope
The first of the three routes is noise. Let \(Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\) independent of \(Y^\star\), mean zero and variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). The hospital has the measure and wants need. The best linear guess of need from the measure is the regression of \(Y^\star\) on \(Y\), whose slope is \[
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y^\star, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star) + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}
= \lambda ,
\] because \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y^\star, \varepsilon) = 0\). The factor \(\lambda\) is between \(0\) and \(1\) and is called the reliability of the measure: the share of its variance that is need rather than noise. When \(Y^\star\) and \(\varepsilon\) are jointly normal with mean zero the regression is the conditional mean, \[
E[Y^\star \mid Y = y] = \lambda y .
\]


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The figure has \(\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 = 1\), so \(\lambda = 1/2\). A patient whose measure is two units above average is expected to be one unit above average in need (the measure has a larger standard deviation than need, so in each variable’s own standard deviations the shrinkage is by \(\sqrt{\lambda}\)). Selecting the top 3% by the measure selects people whose need is high, but less high than their measure says, by the factor \(\lambda\). Manheim and Garrabrant call this the regressional version of Goodhart’s law: pick the largest values of a proxy and you have picked its noise along with its signal. The slope is attenuated toward zero by \(\lambda\), however large the sample. As with ecological regression, more data gives the same wrong answer, with variance in the measure turned into bias in the slope.


Noise and an omitted variable
The slope above has need on the left. In a regression course the noisy measure is usually on the right, as the predictor, and often something is left out as well. Does care improve health? In this subsection \(Y\) is an outcome, not the measure of need. Let \(Y\) be a person’s health next year, \(X^\star\) the number of times they saw a doctor this year, and \(X = X^\star + \varepsilon\) the number they report, with \(\varepsilon\) independent of everything else. Let \(Z\) be how ill they were this year, which is not in the data, and \[
Y = \beta X^\star + \gamma Z + U ,
\] with \(U\) independent of \(X^\star\), \(Z\) and \(\varepsilon\). Someone with data on \(X\) and \(Y\) regresses health on reported visits. The population slope is \[
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
= \frac{\beta \operatorname{Var}(X^\star) + \gamma \operatorname{Cov}(X^\star, Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X^\star) + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}
= \lambda\,(\beta + \gamma\delta),
\qquad
\delta = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X^\star, Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X^\star)} ,
\] where \(\lambda\) is the reliability of the report and \(\delta\) is the slope of illness on visits. With \(\gamma = 0\) this is \(\beta\lambda\), attenuation alone. With no noise, \(\lambda = 1\), it is the slope with a variable left out, \(\beta + \gamma\delta\), whose omitted-variable bias is \(\gamma\delta\).
The two biases work differently. Noise multiplies the slope by \(\lambda\), which is between 0 and 1: it pulls the slope toward zero and never changes its sign. The left-out variable adds \(\gamma\delta\) to \(\beta\) inside the bracket. Its sign is the sign of the product of the two arrows out of \(Z\), and it can change the sign of the slope. Visits help, \(\beta > 0\). The ill visit more, \(\delta > 0\), and are less healthy next year, \(\gamma < 0\), so \(\gamma\delta < 0\). If \(\gamma\delta < -\beta\), the people who visit more are less healthy next year, the slope is negative, and the data say that care does harm. Noise only shrinks that wrong answer toward zero.









The figure has \(\beta = 1/2\). When \(\gamma\delta > 0\) the two biases pull against each other, and the slope can be too large or too small: it is larger than \(\beta\) when \(\gamma\delta > \beta(1 - \lambda)/\lambda\). The classic case is the return to a year of schooling, with earnings for health, years of schooling for visits and ability left out. Ability is usually taken to raise both schooling and earnings, so \(\gamma\delta > 0\). Card (1999, section 3.3 and the abstract) reviews the evidence: the reliability of self-reported schooling is about 0.9, and studies of identical twins suggest a small upward bias from ability, so the two partly offset.
None of \(\lambda\), \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\) comes from the data on \(X\) and \(Y\). The reliability needs a second report of the same quantity, and the term for the left-out variable needs a measure of it or a design that holds it fixed. From \(X\) and \(Y\) alone you cannot tell whether the slope is too large, too small or of the wrong sign.
This is classical noise, independent of everything else. Noise that is related to the true value, to the outcome or to the left-out variable can move the slope in either direction, and so can noise in a variable that is adjusted for, which leaves part of the confounding it was meant to remove. Noise in the outcome is different again: it goes into \(U\), widens the interval around the slope and leaves its center alone.


Need, resources and care-seeking
The hospital selected on cost and wanted need, and the model so far has cost differ from need by an offset and by noise. Cost also depends on other things about a person. Write \[
Y = Y^\star + W + C + \varepsilon ,
\] where \(W\) stands for a person’s resources (insurance that pays, income, transport, time off work, a doctor who records every diagnosis), what turns need into care and care into cost, and \(C\) for care-seeking, how readily a person goes to a doctor at a given level of need. The noise \(\varepsilon\) is the rest: an accident, a test that had to be repeated. Suppose the four are independent and normal with mean zero.
The best guess of each part from the measure is the calculation that gave \(\lambda\). For need, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y^\star, Y) = \operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)\), so \[
E[Y^\star \mid Y = y] = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\, y ,
\] and likewise for \(W\), \(C\) and \(\varepsilon\). The four fractions add up to 1, because \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) is the sum of the four variances. Averaging over the people selected, those with \(Y > t\), gives each part’s mean among them: its share of \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) times their mean cost, \[
E[Y^\star \mid Y > t] = E\big[E[Y^\star \mid Y] \,\big|\, Y > t\big]
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\, E[Y \mid Y > t] .
\] With variances 1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4, the shares are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8. Of the selected’s mean cost above the population mean, half is need, a quarter resources, an eighth care-seeking and an eighth noise. The selected are a mixture: some are there mostly because they are ill, some because they could turn need into care, some because they seek care readily.
Among the selected the parts are negatively related, although they are independent in the population: to clear the threshold with less need, a person needed more of something else. And when the parts are related in the population, the mixture changes. If poorer people are sicker, with the spread of need unchanged, the sickest have fewer resources and generate less cost than their need, and the places go less to need: the hospital’s offset again, inside one group.
Some of the parts are more under a person’s control than others. How readily someone seeks care is partly a choice. Illness, income and where someone lives are much less so. The ability to raise a score without raising what it stands for, gaming in the section on systems that adapt below, is often a resource. A program that selects on the score rewards all of these together.

title: What’s the score?
text:
Reinforcement learning
Notation: this section uses the letters of reinforcement learning: \(S\) state, \(A\) action, \(R\) reward, \(\pi\) policy, \(U\) utility.
An agent observes a state \(S\), takes an action \(A\), and receives a reward \(R\). A policy \(\pi\) is a rule that chooses the action from the state, \(A = \pi(S)\), and learning means changing the policy to make the expected reward, \(E_\pi[R]\), large, where \(E_\pi\) is the expectation when the agent acts by \(\pi\). The utility \(U\) is what we care about. A utilitarian would choose the policy whose expected utility \(E_\pi[U]\) is largest. The agent is given \(R\) instead, because \(R\) can be measured and \(U\) often cannot: in the job center below, \(U\) needs what would have happened without the course. \(R\) and \(U\) can come apart. In the letters of the rest of these notes, \(R\) is \(Y\) and \(U\) is \(Y^\star\).









Amodei and colleagues (2016) use a cleaning robot as a running example. In these letters, the state is what the robot’s camera shows, the actions are where to move and whether to clean, and the utility is a clean room. If the reward is for not seeing any mess, the robot can earn it by closing its eyes, or by covering the mess with something it cannot see through.

  a single row.









Now a variant of the job center and its job-search course, with 100 places on the course, which helps some people more than others. Take the rates that follow as what would happen under assignment to the course or to no course, so that the differences are effects and not a confounded comparison. Of people who worked last year, 70% are in work six months later if they take the course and 64% if they do not; of people who did not work last year, 40% and 14%. The state is a person’s record, the action is to refer or not, and the center is judged on the share of the people it refers who are in work, its placement rate. That rate is its reward. Referring 100 people who worked last year earns a rate of 70% and puts 6 more people in work, on average, than would be in work without the course. Referring 100 who did not earns 40% and puts 26 more in work. A center judged on its placement rate refers the first group; a utilitarian counting the jobs the course creates refers the second, and so serves the people who need the course most.









Choosing people who would have done well anyway is called cream skimming. Heckman, Heinrich and Smith (2002) studied it in US job-training centers funded under the Job Training Partnership Act, which were judged partly on employment rates. They found the short-run measures “weakly, and sometimes perversely, related to long run impacts.” They also found that cream skimming made little difference to the programs’ efficiency, in either direction, unlike the invented numbers above, and concluded: “Opposition to cream skimming must come on equity grounds.” Equity here is about who is served; efficiency is about the total.
The job center chose between two utilities, and the hospital faces the same choice. Its program, the paper says, mostly prevents acute episodes in people with chronic illness. One candidate for \(U\) is how ill a patient is; another is how much the extra care would help them. They pick out different people whenever the care helps some patients more than others, which is the heterogeneity an average treatment effect averages over. Telling the two apart needs an estimate of the program’s effect on each kind of patient, a causal claim that the hospital’s data, on patients it chose to enroll, do not give by themselves. Choosing between them is not an estimate at all: it is a judgment about whose good the program is for, and no label makes it for you.
Each of the four difficulties of utilitarianism becomes a choice someone makes in building such an agent. Defining utility becomes choosing \(R\), a measurable stand-in for \(U\), and in both examples the two come apart. Trading off between people becomes adding the reward up over the people the agent serves; the placement rate counts only the people referred. Judging acts or rules becomes choosing a policy, a rule that treats alike everyone in the same state. Judging each action on its own and judging the rule can give different answers: when a rule has to treat different situations alike, as a model that sees only a few variables about each person does; when places are limited, so that one referral uses a place another person could have had; and when people respond to the rule itself. Predicting consequences becomes choosing a model of what the actions do, which is a causal model.
Is \(E_\pi[U]\) a causal quantity? It can be read as one, the expected utility if the agent’s actions were set by \(\pi\), but that reading needs assumptions beyond those of the interventions met so far, which set a variable to the same value for everyone in a population. Here one agent follows a rule. The people and systems it acts on may respond to what it does, sometimes adversarially, and what happens to one of them can depend on what was done to others. Causal reinforcement learning, a subfield surveyed by Deng, Jiang, Long and Zhang (2023), brings causal models into reinforcement learning.
These letters clash with the ones used for prediction, which most of the course uses.









prediction
reinforcement learning




\(A\)
sensitive attribute: something a person is
action: something an agent does


\(R\)
risk score, with \(\hat Y = 1\{R \ge t\}\)
reward


\(U\)
unobserved variable
utility


\(S\), \(\pi\)
not used
state, policy



If you read about reinforcement learning you will meet these letters with these meanings. New letters invented for this course would teach a convention nobody else uses. Two rules are enough. Material that uses the reinforcement-learning letters says so in one line at the top, as this section does. And the two sets of letters are never mixed inside one diagram or one derivation. A classifier described as an agent takes its prediction \(\hat Y\) as its action, which reinforcement learning would write as \(A\). Mixing the two there would give \(A\) two meanings in one line.

title: What’s the score?
text:
Systems that adapt

When a measure becomes a target
So far the people being measured have done nothing. Now reward the measure. Before the rule, \[
Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon ,
\] and selecting the people with the highest \(Y\) is conditioning: it picks out a group whose need is high, shrunk by \(\lambda\), because the old relation between \(Y\) and \(Y^\star\) still holds among the people picked. After the rule, each person can add an amount \(g \ge 0\) to their own \(Y\), at some cost, without changing \(Y^\star\): \[
Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon + g .
\]


Warning: The `label.size` argument of `geom_label()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.5.0.
i Please use the `linewidth` argument instead.









Replacing the equation that generates \(Y\) is an intervention: a new assignment for one variable, every other line left alone. The relation between \(Y\) and \(Y^\star\) that held before the rule need not hold after it. Which people it fails for depends on who can pay for \(g\).
Who can respond determines what the response does. Compare two cases with the same 300 places for the highest \(Y\). If everyone adds the same \(1\) to their \(Y\), every ranking is unchanged, the same 300 people are selected, and nothing about them has changed: a rewarded measure is not spoiled by the reward alone. If half of the people are able to add \(1\) and the rest cannot, the ranking changes, and it changes toward the people who could respond. The simulation below has ten thousand people, need and noise standard normal, and who is able to add \(1\) unrelated to need. Each panel plots the measure against need, with the cutoff for 300 places dashed and the 300 selected drawn solid. The first two panels are the same picture shifted up by one: the same people are selected. In the third the 300 places go mostly to people who were able to add \(1\), and the selected reach further down in need.









The fall in mean need in the third case is modest, because the people able to add \(1\) were drawn from the same need distribution as everyone else; what changes most is who the places go to. The first two cases select the same people, which is the check that it is the difference in response, not the response itself, that moves the allocation. In the paper’s setting the equivalent would be a hospital that rewards patients, or their doctors, for a high score, after which the score measures who responded to the reward.


   mean_y mean_need 
 3.173319  1.686755 


Two formal versions of a system that adapts are in the reading’s authors’ own work.
Strategic classification (Hardt, Megiddo, Papadimitriou and Wootters 2016). A classifier is published. Each person then changes their features, at a cost that depends on the change, to get the label they want. The classifier is scored on the features as changed, against each person’s true label, which is fixed by the features as they were before the change; so every response is gaming, and the design problem is a classifier that stays accurate when everyone games it. The paper gives efficient algorithms for a natural class of cost functions and shows the general problem is hard.
Performative prediction (Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner and Hardt 2020). A prediction that is acted on can change the thing it predicts: a traffic forecast changes which roads people take, and a forecast that a loan will default can make it default. The authors call such predictions performative. The distribution the model is evaluated on depends on the model deployed, by whatever mechanism, and the labels can move along with the features. The question is what retraining on the data a model induces converges to, a model they call performatively stable, and whether that point has low loss. They give conditions under which it does, and show that strategic classification is the special case in which the mechanism is individuals responding to a published rule.
Gaming and improvement. Miller, Milli and Hardt (2020) separate responses to a rule that game it from responses that improve what it stands for, and show that designing a rule that rewards improvement “must inevitably solve a non-trivial causal inference problem.” The example here is ours. Take a course judged by its students’ test scores. Practicing raises skill, and skill raises the score; memorizing old papers raises the score without touching skill. Each graph is a claim someone could dispute.









Whether a response to a rule is gaming or improvement depends on the causal model. If the feature a person changes raises the outcome, the change is improvement, and \(Y^\star\) rises with \(Y\); if it changes only the measure, the change is gaming, as in the second graph. The graph says which features can affect the outcome at all; whether a given change raises it, and by how much, needs the model’s equations too. A rule meant to reward improvement has to know which, and that is a causal inference problem; the authors show that any procedure for designing such rules has to solve one. Conditioning is not intervening, a third time: the rule intervenes on the people it is applied to, and what their response does depends on the graph, not on what the rule’s designer intended.


Engagement
Notation: this section uses the letters of reinforcement learning: \(S\) state, \(A\) action, \(R\) reward, \(\pi\) policy, \(U\) utility.
A recommender system is an agent. Its state is what it knows about a user, its action is what to show next, and its reward is whatever the platform can measure about the response: a click, a view, time watched, a share. In August 2012 YouTube told its creators that its discovery features had been “designed to drive views,” which rewarded videos that got clicked over videos that kept viewers watching, and that it would rank by watch time instead. A platform’s reward is engagement in some form. A user’s utility is something else: being informed, or entertained, on their own terms, and not manipulated. The two need not conflict: a change that keeps viewers watching can serve them too. Where they do conflict, where raising \(U\) would lower \(R\), a platform whose revenue rises with \(R\) has a reason not to, and nobody inside has to decide to leave the gap open; the reward decides for them. The post describes one change of reward, not the incentives behind it; that reading is mine.
Selecting the largest of \(n\) is the selection half of this story: a feed shows the most extreme of \(n\) items. This is the optimization half: a feed that ranks by \(R\) changes what gets made, because the people who make it write for the score.

title: What’s the score?
text:
Lenses
What are we optimizing or predicting? Cost, standing in for need. Citations, standing in for a contribution. A placement rate, standing in for jobs created. Views, or watch time, standing in for a viewer’s good. In each case the first word is what the system can measure and the second is what someone wanted; the system’s designer chose the first and the system optimized it.
Who bears the error? A threshold at the 97th percentile makes two errors, a place used on someone who did not need it and a person left out who did, and trades them against each other, whether by a judgment about their costs or by how many places the program has. An offset in the measure moves the second error onto one group, the one whose costs were lower at the same need. The cleaning robot’s owner bears the difference between the robot’s reward and a clean room; the job seekers a center did not refer bear the difference between its placement rate and the jobs the course would have created.
What can be changed, and how? What things are considered “controlled for” or “held fixed,” and is that realistic? This lens is new this week, and it is causal modeling put as a question. Benefit is an effect: it compares the same patient with the extra care and without it, holding the patient fixed. A slope of health on reported visits is read as the effect of a visit with illness held fixed; illness is not in the data, so nothing held it fixed. The lens also asks what the people scored can change: how readily they seek care is easier for them to change than how ill they are. Goodhart’s law is the case where something was assumed to stay fixed and did not: a rule rewarding the score assumed that the relation between the score and need would hold, and the people scored changed it. Strategic classification holds the true label fixed while people change their features; performative prediction drops that assumption and lets the whole distribution move.
And why? A measure is chosen because it can be measured. Cost is in the billing system and need is not. Views are counted and a viewer’s understanding is not. The choice is made once, often by a vendor, and afterward nobody has to make it again; the score makes it for them.

title: What’s the score?
text:
For the class

Exercises, problems and simulation
The exercises, done on students’ own time, compute who is selected under an offset at a new threshold and with a fixed number of places, derive \(\lambda\) from the covariance algebra above, then the slope \(\lambda(\beta + \gamma\delta)\) with numbers that make it too large, too small and of the wrong sign, and simulate it. In class, problem 1 draws the graph of need, resources and care-seeking with selection on cost and computes each part’s mean among the selected, and the class simulates the selection, with gaming that depends on resources. Problem 2 changes the label to the number of active chronic conditions and asks what reaches it and what happens once it is paid on.
